title: Pentagon's latest UFO file release revives a long-standing Roswell mystery
excerpt: Pentagon’s latest UFO file release has reportedly revived a long-standing Roswell mystery. The release included Walter Haut's eyewitness account of the alleged UFO crash that reportedly occurred near Roswell, New Mexico, in July 1947.
content:

Pentagon’s latest UFO file release has reportedly revived a long-standing Roswell mystery. The release included Walter Haut's eyewitness account of the alleged UFO crash that reportedly occurred near Roswell, New Mexico, in July 1947.

News Nation revealed that in 1947, Haut worked as the public information officer at the Roswell Army Air Field. There he issued a press release to announce that the government had recovered a flying disc. Soon afterward, the military changed its explanation and declared that a weather balloon had crashed instead. However, in an affidavit dated December 26, 2002, Haut revealed what he claimed he had actually witnessed during the incident.

A few days earlier, TV host Dr. Phil McGraw also opened up in an American Thought Leaders interview about 50 crashed alien aircraft and revealed that these retained spacecraft were made of metallurgical substances.

Continue reading more about the story.

Pentagon's new UFO files brought the Roswell crash mystery back into focus

Pentagon's seventh batch reportedly revealed Walter Haut's eyewitness account of the alleged UFO crash that happened near Roswell, New Mexico, in July 1947.

News Nation revealed that rancher William Brazel discovered debris near his ranch. At that time, Brazel was unaware of the trend because he didn't have access to a phone or radio. After reporting the discovery to the local sheriff, the sheriff passed the information on to the U.S. Air Force. The Air Force initially released a statement and claimed that military personnel had recovered debris from a flying disc.

Haut recalled that his superiors instructed him to leave and stay out of sight because his office was receiving an overwhelming number of calls from across the world. Before departing, he said he briefly entered a hangar where he saw a metallic, egg-shaped object along with two small, child-sized bodies with large heads covered with canvas tarpaulin. Haut said,

"I am convinced that what I personally observed was some type of craft and its crew from outer space."

Haut's affidavit claimed that the debris linked to the alleged UFO crash was removed from an office and later replaced with parts from a weather balloon and a radar kite. However, in 1978, a retired military officer challenged the weather balloon explanation and described it as recovered debris that might have belonged to extraterrestrials. His claim helped fuel a conspiracy theory that continued for decades.

Haut also mentioned that he was permitted to visit at least one recovery site during the military’s cleanup operation. He revealed that later he brought some of the recovered wreckage back to the base and displayed it in his office.

The affidavit included in the latest files had been partially redacted, with the names of Haut and several other military officials removed from the document. The account appeared within a 2008 report prepared by a contractor for the Defense Intelligence Agency.
